idiom_name: static member factory functions (Named Constructor idiom)
implementation_notes: Constructors are distinguishable only by parameter types, so each construction route becomes a public static member function with a meaningful name and every constructor is made private (protected if subclassing is intended). Since C++17 a factory that returns a prvalue constructs directly in the caller's storage - guaranteed copy elision - so returning by value costs exactly what a constructor call costs; std::make_unique and std::make_shared are the standard library's own named constructors and show the same shape. Keep the classic form when signatures would otherwise collide (Point::rectangular vs Point::polar) or when creation must enforce allocation, validation or registration policy.
pitfalls: A factory that allocates must return an owner (std::unique_ptr/std::shared_ptr); handing back a raw owning pointer reintroduces exactly the leak the factory was meant to prevent.

std::make_shared/std::make_unique cannot call a non-public constructor, so a private constructor forces the factory to write new itself - a second allocation for the control block and the exception-safety reasoning that make_* otherwise takes off your hands.
Any construction path left public (free function, extra constructor, aggregate initialization) is a bypass route, and the invariant the named constructors enforce stops holding.

variants.name: Factories returning smart pointers
variants.implementation_notes: When creation must also decide ownership, the named constructors return std::unique_ptr or std::shared_ptr instead of values; the constructor stays private and the factory performs the allocation itself, because std::make_unique and std::make_shared require public access to the selected constructor. This keeps the deleter and deallocation policy inside the type and lets a failed creation return nullptr or an expected-like result, at the price of give up make_shared's single-allocation layout (the control block becomes a second allocation). Choose it for resource owning types (connections, buffers, node graphs) rather than for small value types.
pitfalls: make_shared/make_unique cannot reach a private constructor (they require public access to the selected constructor), so the factory must write new directly and loses the single-allocation shared_ptr layout.
Returning unique_ptr by value is correct, but returning it as a reference or a raw pointer destroys the ownership contract the factory exists to express.
A factory that returns shared_ptr invites accidental sharing of mutable objects; return shared_ptr<const T> or document the sharing contract when the object is not thread-safe.
